prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Employing density-functional calculations we study single and double graphene layers on Si- and C-terminated 1x1-6H-SiC surfaces. We show that, in contrast to earlier assumptions, the first carbon layer is covalently bonded to the substrate, and cannot be responsible for the graphene-type electronic spectrum observed experimentally. The characteristic spectrum of free-standing graphene appears with the second carbon layer, which exhibits a weak van der Waals bonding to the underlying structure. For Si-terminated substrate, the interface is metallic, whereas on C-face it is semiconducting or semimetallic for single or double graphene coverage, respectively.

outputs.L2: Using density-functional calculations, we investigate one and two graphene layers supported on Si- and C-terminated 1×1-6H-SiC surfaces. Our results indicate that, contrary to previous assumptions, the initial carbon layer forms covalent bonds with the substrate and therefore cannot account for the graphene-like electronic spectrum seen in experiments. Density-functional calculations were performed to investigate the structural and electronic properties of single and double graphene layers on both Si-terminated and C-terminated \(1 \times 1\) \(6H\)-SiC surfaces. The study shows that the interaction between graphene and the SiC substrate depends strongly on the termination of the surface and on the number of carbon layers present.

A key result is that the first carbon layer does not behave like an isolated graphene sheet. Instead, it is covalently bonded to the SiC substrate. This finding contradicts earlier assumptions that the first carbon layer on SiC is only weakly attached and already possesses the electronic properties of free-standing graphene. Because of this strong bonding, the electronic structure of the first carbon layer is significantly modified by the substrate.

As a consequence, the first carbon layer cannot be responsible for the graphene-like electronic spectrum observed experimentally. In particular, the characteristic electronic features of free-standing graphene, such as the linear dispersion near the Fermi level, are suppressed or strongly altered when the carbon layer is directly bonded to the SiC surface.

The calculations indicate that the graphene-like electronic spectrum appears only when a second carbon layer is added. This second layer is not covalently bonded to the substrate; instead, it interacts weakly with the first carbon layer through van der Waals forces. Because it is electronically more decoupled from the SiC substrate, the second layer can recover the characteristic electronic behavior of free-standing graphene.

The electronic properties of the interface also depend on whether the SiC surface is Si-terminated or C-terminated. For the Si-terminated surface, the interface remains metallic. In contrast, the C-terminated surface is semiconducting when covered by a single carbon layer, but becomes semimetallic when a second carbon layer is present. These results demonstrate that both surface termination and graphene thickness play crucial roles in determining the electronic structure of graphene grown on SiC.

Density-functional theory calculations were used to investigate the structural and electronic properties of one and two carbon layers on the Si- and C-terminated \(1 \times 1\) surfaces of 6H-SiC. The purpose of the study was to clarify how graphene-like electronic states develop when carbon layers form on silicon carbide, and to determine whether the first carbon layer at the interface can truly be regarded as graphene.

The calculations show that the first carbon layer does not behave like an isolated graphene sheet. Instead, it forms strong covalent bonds with the underlying SiC substrate. This bonding significantly modifies the carbon layer’s atomic and electronic structure, destroying the characteristic linear \(\pi\)-band dispersion associated with free-standing graphene. As a result, the first carbon layer acts more like an interfacial buffer layer than an electronically active graphene sheet.

When a second carbon layer is added, the situation changes substantially. The second layer is only weakly coupled to the first carbon layer and is much less affected by the SiC substrate. Its electronic band structure closely resembles that of free-standing graphene, including the characteristic graphene-like \(\pi\) bands near the Fermi level. This indicates that the graphene electronic spectrum observed experimentally does not originate from the first carbon layer directly bonded to SiC, but from an additional carbon layer that forms above the interfacial buffer layer.

The results therefore provide an important interpretation of graphene growth on SiC. They suggest that, on both Si- and C-terminated 6H-SiC surfaces, the initial carbon layer primarily serves to passivate or reconstruct the substrate surface through covalent bonding. Only after a second, more weakly bonded carbon layer is formed do the electronic properties typical of graphene emerge. This explains why experimental signatures of graphene, such as graphene-like bands in photoemission measurements, are associated with multilayer formation rather than with the first carbon layer at the SiC interface.
outputs.L5:
Employing SiC, or silicon carbide, is becoming increasingly important in modern technology. The material is known for its high thermal conductivity, excellent strength, and resistance to extreme temperatures. These qualities make SiC especially useful in power electronics, electric vehicles, aerospace systems, and industrial equipment.

The main advantage of SiC is its ability to operate efficiently under harsh conditions where traditional silicon materials may fail. Employing SiC in semiconductor devices can reduce energy losses, improve performance, and allow systems to become smaller and more reliable. For example, SiC-based power modules are widely used in electric vehicle chargers and renewable energy systems because they support faster switching and higher voltage operation.

The future of SiC looks promising as industries continue to demand more efficient and durable materials. By employing SiC in advanced applications, manufacturers can improve energy efficiency, reduce heat generation, and support the development of cleaner technologies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a computational materials science paper about DFT studies of one and two graphene layers on Si- and C-terminated 6H-SiC(0001) surfaces, emphasizing bonding and electronic structure.
counterfactuals.output: We present density functional theory calculations of one and two graphene layers on Si- and C-terminated 6H-SiC(0001) surfaces to elucidate interface bonding and the resulting electronic structure. On the Si-terminated surface, the first carbon layer forms strong covalent bonds to surface Si atoms, producing a buffer layer with disrupted graphene π states and no freestanding Dirac cone. A second graphene layer is electronically decoupled to a greater extent and recovers graphene-like bands, modified by substrate-induced doping and interface potential. In contrast, graphene on the C-terminated surface exhibits weaker interfacial bonding, reduced structural perturbation, and more readily preserves characteristic π-band dispersion even for the first layer. The calculations reveal a strong dependence of graphene electronic properties on substrate termination, interfacial registry, and layer number, providing microscopic insight into epitaxial graphene growth on SiC and the emergence of quasi-freestanding graphene behavior.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize findings on graphene grown on 1x1 6H-SiC surfaces, comparing Si-face and C-face terminations and explaining when the graphene-like spectrum appears.
counterfactuals.output:
Findings for graphene on ideal \(1\times1\) 6H-SiC surfaces can be summarized as follows:

- **Si-face termination: 6H-SiC(0001)**  
  The first carbon layer deposited on the Si-terminated surface interacts strongly with the substrate. Surface Si dangling bonds form covalent bonds with the carbon layer, so this first layer is not electronically equivalent to free-standing graphene. Its \(\pi\) bands are strongly hybridized with substrate states, and the usual graphene-like Dirac spectrum is absent or strongly distorted. This interfacial carbon layer behaves more like a **buffer layer**.

- **C-face termination: 6H-SiC(\(000\bar{1}\))**  
  The interaction is generally weaker and structurally different than on the Si-face, but for an ideal unreconstructed \(1\times1\) surface the first carbon layer can still be significantly affected by the substrate. The details depend on bonding geometry, but the main point is that the layer directly in contact with the SiC surface is not always a fully free graphene sheet.

- **When the graphene-like spectrum appears**  
  A recognizable graphene-like band structure—linear \(\pi\) and \(\pi^\*\) bands near the Fermi level, resembling the Dirac cone of isolated graphene—appears only when there is at least one carbon layer sufficiently decoupled from the substrate. In practice, this means that the **first interfacial layer passivates or bonds to the SiC surface**, and the **next carbon layer above it** exhibits the graphene-like spectrum.

Thus, for ideal \(1\times1\) 6H-SiC surfaces, the carbon layer directly contacting the substrate is usually strongly modified by bonding and hybridization, especially on the Si-face. The “true” graphene electronic signature emerges from the second layer or higher, once the substrate interaction is screened by the interfacial buffer layer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a journal-style abstract stating that the first carbon layer on SiC is covalently bonded rather than graphene-like, while the second layer recovers free-standing graphene electronic properties.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the electronic structure of the first two carbon layers formed on SiC during epitaxial graphene growth. The results show that the interfacial, first carbon layer is not electronically equivalent to free-standing graphene: instead, it is strongly coupled to the SiC substrate through covalent bonding, which disrupts the characteristic graphene π bands and suppresses Dirac-cone behavior. This interfacial layer therefore acts as a structurally graphene-like but electronically inactive buffer layer. In contrast, the second carbon layer is largely decoupled from the substrate and exhibits the hallmark electronic properties of free-standing graphene, including restored π-band dispersion and Dirac-like low-energy states. These findings establish that graphene-like electronic behavior on SiC emerges only from the second carbon layer, while the first carbon layer serves primarily as a covalently bonded template mediating epitaxial growth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal scientific language, describe density-functional calculations of single and double graphene layers on SiC, including differences between metallic, semiconducting, and semimetallic interfaces.
counterfactuals.output:
Density-functional theory (DFT) calculations for single- and double-layer graphene on silicon carbide are typically formulated using periodic slab models of the SiC surface, with one or two graphene sheets adsorbed on the terminating SiC bilayer. The atomic coordinates are relaxed until residual forces are small, and the resulting electronic structure is analyzed through band dispersions, projected densities of states, charge transfer, and real-space charge-density differences. Because the lattice constants of graphene and SiC are incommensurate, commensurate supercells or reconstructed surface cells are used to approximate the epitaxial registry.

For a **single graphene layer on SiC**, the electronic structure depends strongly on the chemical nature of the interface. If the carbon layer is directly bonded to the SiC substrate, as in a buffer-layer configuration on the Si-terminated surface, hybridization between graphene \(p_z\) orbitals and Si dangling-bond states can destroy the ideal graphene Dirac cone. The layer may then no longer behave as electronically free-standing graphene; instead, interface-induced states and covalent bonding modify the \(\pi\)-band dispersion, open gaps, or shift the Fermi level. Charge transfer from the substrate can produce \(n\)-type doping, while different terminations or passivation schemes can yield weaker coupling and more graphene-like bands.

For a **double graphene layer on SiC**, the lower carbon layer often acts as an interfacial or buffer layer, screening the upper layer from the substrate. The second graphene sheet consequently exhibits a band structure closer to that of isolated monolayer or bilayer graphene, although it may still be doped by electrostatic charge transfer from the interface. In Bernal-stacked bilayer configurations, the low-energy bands near the \(K\) point acquire the characteristic bilayer form, and substrate-induced symmetry breaking can open a small gap between valence and conduction bands. Thus, adding a second layer generally reduces direct substrate hybridization and restores more intrinsic graphene-like electronic behavior.

The calculations distinguish three limiting classes of interface electronic structure:

1. **Metallic interfaces.**  
   Metallic behavior arises when unsaturated Si or C dangling bonds at the SiC surface generate bands crossing the Fermi level. These interface states coexist with, hybridize with, or obscure the graphene \(\pi\) bands. In such systems the Fermi level is pinned by substrate-derived states, and the electronic properties are governed not only by graphene but also by the chemically active interface. Metallic interfaces therefore exhibit finite density of states at \(E_F\), strong charge redistribution, and often substantial perturbation of the graphene Dirac spectrum.

2. **Semiconducting interfaces.**  
   A semiconducting interface is obtained when surface dangling bonds are saturated or when the bonding geometry removes interface states from the SiC band gap. In this case the SiC substrate retains a gap at the Fermi level, and the graphene-derived states dominate the low-energy electronic structure. The interaction may still shift the Dirac point relative to \(E_F\), producing electron or hole doping, and may open a small gap if sublattice symmetry is broken. Compared with metallic interfaces, semiconducting interfaces produce weaker Fermi-level pinning and allow more controllable graphene-like transport.

3. **Semimetallic interfaces.**  
   Semimetallic behavior corresponds to the case in which the low-energy spectrum is dominated by graphene \(\pi\) and \(\pi^\ast\) bands meeting near the Fermi level, with little or no density of substrate states at \(E_F\). The system then resembles free-standing graphene, with a Dirac cone for monolayer graphene or parabolic low-energy bands for Bernal bilayer graphene. Small deviations from ideal semimetallicity may occur because of charge transfer, interlayer coupling, strain, or weak substrate potentials.

Overall, DFT calculations show that the electronic character of graphene on SiC is controlled primarily by interface bonding and surface passivation. A chemically active, dangling-bond-rich interface tends to be metallic and strongly perturbs graphene. A saturated or reconstructed interface is semiconducting and preserves the SiC gap. When substrate states are absent near the Fermi level and graphene \(\pi\) states dominate, the combined system behaves semimetallically, with electronic properties close to those of intrinsic graphene. The transition from one to two graphene layers generally weakens substrate influence on the outermost layer, making bilayer systems more graphene-like than directly bonded monolayers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a short research abstract on epitaxial graphene on Si- and C-terminated 6H-SiC, focusing on substrate bonding, van der Waals interaction of the second layer, and the resulting electronic spectra.
counterfactuals.output: Epitaxial graphene on the Si- and C-terminated surfaces of 6H-SiC exhibits markedly different interfacial bonding and electronic behavior. On the Si-terminated face, the first carbon layer forms a strongly bonded buffer layer through partial covalent attachment to surface Si atoms, disrupting its graphene-like π electronic structure. The subsequent carbon layer is largely decoupled from the substrate and interacts primarily through van der Waals forces with the buffer layer, enabling the recovery of characteristic graphene bands near the Fermi level, including a Dirac-like dispersion that may be shifted by substrate-induced doping. In contrast, growth on the C-terminated face generally involves weaker interfacial bonding and rotational stacking disorder, which reduces interlayer electronic coupling and promotes quasi-freestanding graphene-like spectra even for relatively thin films. The second layer on both terminations is governed predominantly by noncovalent interlayer interactions, but the strength of substrate perturbation differs substantially between the two faces. These differences produce distinct electronic spectra: the Si-face shows buffer-layer-induced interface states and doped monolayer graphene bands, whereas the C-face more readily exhibits decoupled graphene π bands with reduced substrate hybridization. Understanding the balance between covalent substrate bonding and van der Waals interlayer coupling is therefore essential for controlling the electronic structure of epitaxial graphene on polar SiC surfaces.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
